name: West Germanic
region: The North Sea coast and the Rhine, Weser and Elbe basins; later Britain
defining_innovation: West Germanic gemination: a consonant other than r doubled after a short vowel before *j (Gothic satjan, Old English settan 'to set').

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body: West Germanic is the branch left behind on the continent between the North Sea and the Alps after East Germanic speakers moved away and Nordic speech went its own way. It has the most speakers of any Germanic branch today, including English, German and Dutch, but in its early centuries it is almost silent. Apart from a few runic inscriptions and names, the first real texts come in the 7th and 8th centuries, by which point the daughter languages are already distinct.

chapters.title: A Unity or a Continuum?
chapters.body:
Whether West Germanic was ever a single language is one of the family's longest-running arguments. In the 1940s Friedrich Maurer proposed five early Germanic groups based on archaeology and tribal names: North Sea, Weser-Rhine, Elbe, Oder-Vistula and North Germanic. On that view, 'West Germanic' is a later convergence of neighbours rather than a node on the tree.

The case for a real West Germanic ancestor rests on shared changes that are hard to explain as coincidence. **Gemination** doubled consonants before `*j`: Gothic *satjan* but Old Saxon *settian*, Old English *settan*. Final `*-z` was lost: Gothic *dags*, Old Norse *dagr* but Old English *dæg*, Old High German *tag*. There are shared morphological innovations as well, such as the second-person singular past-tense ending *-i*. Old English *nōme* and Old High German *nāmi* 'you took' contrast with Gothic *namt*. Ringe and Taylor (2014) conclude that these add up to a genuine clade.

chapters.title: The Second Consonant Shift
chapters.body: Between about the 6th and 8th centuries the southern dialects went through a second round of consonant shifting: English *pound*, *water*, *make* against German *Pfund*, *Wasser*, *machen*. The shift is strongest in the south and fades northward in a series of staggered isoglosses, the 'Rhenish fan'. The best known of them, the *Benrath line* (*maken* : *machen*), still divides Low German and Dutch from High German. Because the shift is what defines High German, its turning point is recorded on that branch.

chapters.title: Daughter Branches
chapters.body:
West Germanic is conventionally divided into three groups:

- **Anglo-Frisian**: English and Frisian, the one daughter branch covered in depth here
- **Low Franconian and Low German**: Dutch, Afrikaans, Low Saxon, which did not take part in the second shift
- **High German**: Standard German, Swiss German, Bavarian, Luxembourgish, and Yiddish, which formed through the contact of medieval German with Hebrew, Aramaic and Slavic

The exact internal groupings, especially the position of Old Saxon, which shares several 'North Sea' features with English and Frisian, are themselves disputed.

turning_points.title: West Germanic emerges
turning_points.description: The continental dialects south of Scandinavia develop shared innovations of their own. Whether they did this as a unified language or as a network of neighbouring dialects is a central dispute (see Contested Classifications).

sources.citation: Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Maurer, Friedrich. 1942. Nordgermanen und Alemannen. Strasbourg: Hünenburg.

turning_points.title: West Germanic gemination
turning_points.description: Consonants other than `r` are doubled after a short vowel before `*j`: `*satjan-` → Old English *settan*, Old Saxon *settian* 'to set'. The doubling often outlived the `j` that caused it: Gothic *bidjan* 'to ask' against Old English *biddan*.

sources.citation: Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.date: Before the earliest West Germanic texts
turning_points.title: Loss of final *-z
turning_points.description: Proto-Germanic final `*-z` disappears in West Germanic, while Gothic keeps it as `-s` and Norse as `-r`: `*dagaz` 'day' → Old English *dæg*, Old High German *tag*, against Gothic *dags* and Old Norse *dagr*.

sources.citation: Fulk, R. D. 2018. A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.

turning_points.title: Franks in Gaul
turning_points.description: Frankish rule over northern Gaul leaves a Germanic layer in Gallo-Romance: Old French *guerre* 'war' (from Frankish `*werra`), *blanc* 'white', and *jardin* 'garden'. It may also have influenced French phonology, although that is less certain. The Frankish-speaking elite eventually adopts Romance, while in the north-east Frankish dialects continue into Dutch.

sources.citation: Harbert, Wayne. 2007. The Germanic Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Latin alphabet via the missions
turning_points.description: Christian missions bring the Latin alphabet into use for Old English and Old High German. English scribes added letters for sounds Latin lacked: `þ` and `ƿ` (wynn), both taken from runes, `ð`, and `æ`.

sources.citation: Harbert, Wayne. 2007. The Germanic Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: West Germanic as a single ancestral language, and not a later convergence of separate groups
contested_classifications.evidence_for: A set of shared innovations that is hard to attribute to chance: gemination before `*j`, loss of final `*-z`, the second-person singular past-tense ending *-i*, and several changes to pronouns and verb classes. Ringe and Taylor (2014) argue that together they require a common West Germanic ancestor.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Maurer's five-group model and later continuum approaches read the same features as spreading between already distinct neighbours. Some of the innovations are missing, or only partly present, at the edges of the area. It is also hard to find a time and place where one West Germanic speech community could have existed.

sources.citation: Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Maurer, Friedrich. 1942. Nordgermanen und Alemannen. Strasbourg: Hünenburg.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: North Sea Germanic (Ingvaeonic) as a genetic subgroup: Old English, Old Frisian and Old Saxon descend from one ancestor within West Germanic
contested_classifications.evidence_for: The three share distinctive changes, most famously the loss of a nasal before a fricative with lengthening of the vowel: Old English *gōs* 'goose', *ūs* 'us', *fīf* 'five', and Old Saxon *ūs*, *fīf*, against German *Gans*, *uns*, *fünf*. They also share a single verb ending for all persons of the plural, and pronouns without a final *r* (Old English *wē*, *hē* against German *wir*, *er*).
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Old Saxon shows these features unevenly and otherwise patterns with the continental dialects, so most scholars treat 'North Sea Germanic' as a zone where features spread along the coast rather than a node of the tree. The features are real, but the genealogical reading is disputed.

sources.citation: Nielsen, Hans Frede. 1989. The Germanic Languages: Origins and Early Dialectal Interrelations. Tuscaloosa: University of Alabama Press.
Stiles, Patrick V. 1995. Remarks on the 'Anglo-Frisian' thesis. In Friesische Studien II (NOWELE Supplement 12). Odense: Odense University Press.
